newsitem.title: USA: Fed to face barrage of criticism if it hikes rates.
newsitem.headline: Fed to face barrage of criticism if it hikes rates.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

If Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan thinks the central bank came in for heavy criticism after its recent interest rate rise, he had better be braced for a barrage if it increases rates again next week.
An unusual alliance of corporations and labour unions, conservatives and liberals is already lining up to attack the Fed if it raises rates further.

"There will be a great outcry," said Roger Hickey, co-director of the liberal Campaign for America's Future. "And it will be more than just warnings from members of Congress. You're going to see a real public mobilisation."
Fed critics argue that higher interest rates will only serve to slow the economy and are unnecessary because inflation is low and stable.

The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday to consider whether to raise interest rates again. At its last meeting in March, the panel increased short-term rates for the first time in more than two years, bumping them up by a quarter percentage point.

In a speech last week in New York, Greenspan acknowledged that the March rate rise attracted an unusual amount of criticism but defended the move as a small prudent step to ensure against the risk of higher inflation.

Analysts described the tone of the speech as defensive. In a sign of how sensitive the Fed chairman is to criticism, he mailed a copy of his remarks to the more than 60 lawmakers who wrote him last month complaining about the March rate rise.

A Fed official, who declined to be identified, said he had been surprised by the level of criticism the central bank has come in for, given the strength of the economy. The economy grew at a 5.6 percent annualized clip in the first quarter, its fastest pace in more than nine years.

But the Fed official said the complaints would not deter policymakers from raising rates again, if they thought that necessary to keep the economy from overheating. He said the Fed was not out to kill growth, but rather avoid a boom-bust economic cycle and thus extend the six-year-old expansion.

"It's hard to fault the Federal Reserve," said Greenspan's predecessor, Paul Volcker, adding, "It's a little bit discouraging to me to see the amount of, I don't know if it's nitpicking or more, about the very small move that they made."

What is perhaps most disturbing for Greenspan is that the complaints have not just come from Democrats, but Republicans as well. Greenspan is a long-time Republican who was first named Fed Chairman by former President Ronald Reagan in 1987.

In an interview with Reuters earlier this week, the Republican Chairman of the Congressional Joint Economic criticised the Fed for raising rates in March and said he saw no reason for a further credit tightening next week.
"There is no real evidence of inflation to justify Federal Reserve increases in interest rates," Representative Jim Saxton from New Jersey said.
Hickey, from the Campaign for America's Future, said that lawmakers are worried because they fear that further Fed rate hikes could undermine their efforts to balance the budget.

If the economy slows sharply because the higher rates make it more expensive for companies and consumers to borrow and spend, that would reduce government tax revenues and raise spending on unemployment and other public programmes.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, speaking to reporters after a speech here on Thursday, steered clear of commenting on the recent spate of criticism of the Fed. But he had high praise in general for Greenspan.

"Alan Greenspan has been an outstanding Fed Chairman," Rubin said, adding that the Clinton administration supports the independence of the central bank and does not comment on its interest rate decisions.
The complaints about higher interest rates have not just come from lawmakers. Companies and their unions also have criticised the central bank.

Jerry Jasinowski, President of the National Association of Manufacturers, said the group wrote Greenspan earlier this month arguing against rate hikes, in part because economic growth is likely to slow down on its own in coming months.

Thomas Palley, Assistant Director of Public Policy at the 78-union-strong AFL-CIO labour federation, agreed that the Fed should stand pat and not be worried about recent fast growth. "We should read this as good news, not bad news," he said.
